title: Colorado City Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Colorado City wells have a 250-foot median depth, with finished well costs commonly modeled at $14,800-$25,800.
h1: Colorado City, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Colorado City means dealing with a plains well system that varies substantially from lot to lot. Colorado DWR records show 532 permitted wells within the local study area, although only 333 are recorded as constructed. Of those, 361 report a total depth and 146 report a pump yield.

The local record points to wells commonly completed in alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, with many permits naming an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. A neighboring well is useful evidence, but it is not a guarantee for your parcel. Confirm the permit, water rights, septic layout, access, and expected drilling depth before closing or starting construction.

sections.heading: Colorado City well depth depends on the local formation
sections.html:
The median permitted well depth near Colorado City is 250 feet. The middle half runs from 95 to 475 feet, which is a wide enough spread to matter when comparing drilling bids. The 90th percentile is 605 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,405 feet.

Depths are distributed across the area rather than clustering tightly: 27% are under 100 feet, 29% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 33% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 11% exceed 600 feet. For a bid, ask what depth is included, how extra footage is priced, and what casing and grout are included. Alluvium can differ sharply from fractured rock over short distances.

sections.heading: What a Colorado City well may produce
sections.html:
Among the local records that report pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 6.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. That is generally a workable range for ordinary household use, but the number is a test result, not a promise of continuous supply or pressure at the house.

59% of reported wells fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 28% report more than 15 gallons per minute. The low-yield tail is smaller but important: 2% report under 1 gallon per minute, and 11% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Ask for the yield test, recovery information, storage-tank plan, and pump sizing before assuming irrigation or livestock use is practical.

sections.heading: Colorado City water levels and the record over time
sections.html:
The median reported static water level is 170 feet below the surface, with the middle half ranging from 30 to 309 feet. A shallow water level does not automatically mean a shallow well. The well may be drilled deeper for a reliable completion, and water levels can vary with location, season, pumping, and measurement method.

The decade record shows a median measured level of 203 feet below surface in the 2010s and 105 feet in the 2020s. That change suggests water was measured shallower in the newer group, not that the water table is dropping. Only 37 wells report a static water level, so this is a limited comparison rather than a basin-wide trend. Get a current measurement from the specific well when evaluating an existing home.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Colorado City, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity stretches across several generations. Records show 9 permits in the 1950s, 11 in the 1960s, 52 in the 1970s, 48 in the 1980s, 99 in the 1990s, 95 in the 2000s, 61 in the 2010s, and 34 in the 2020s. The newest permit year in the record is 2025.

The most active names in these records are Spradlin Drilling (Spradlin, Wayne) with 66 wells, Reeves, Mark with 52, and Arkansas Valley Drilling (Moore, Todd A.) with 47. These records help identify local experience, but they do not replace current licensing, references, a written scope, or a site-specific estimate.

sections.heading: A realistic Colorado City well drilling budget
sections.html:
For the local alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 250-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models at about $8,800 to $13,800. That is not the complete project price.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $14,800 to $25,800 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, additional casing, unusual geology, or a longer utility run can increase the bid. Ask whether the estimate includes mobilization, casing, grout, development, yield testing, permits, abandonment of a dry hole, and connection to the building. Compare bids on the same scope rather than on footage rate alone.

sections.heading: Risks to check before drilling or building near Colorado City
sections.html:
The main well risks are variable depth, low yield, and the possibility that a hole does not perform as expected. Fractured-bedrock wells can be unpredictable, and the local records show a broad depth range. A low-yield well may still support a home with storage, but it should be designed around measured production and recovery rather than an optimistic estimate.

There are 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites mapped within about 10 miles, along with 1 historic mine feature and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not establish contamination at your lot. Test existing water for bacteria, nitrates, and locally relevant contaminants before relying on it. Check septic setbacks, replacement-area needs, driveway access, power routes, grading, and building location early. A domestic well permit is not the same as unlimited irrigation or commercial water authorization.

sections.heading: A practical lot review for Colorado City and nearby areas
sections.html:
Before buying, pull the DWR permit and construction records for the property and nearby wells. Compare depth, aquifer name, yield, static level, casing, and well age. The records most often name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer with 486 wells; 32 name the Dakota and 4 name Dakota Sandstone. No local records name a Denver Basin aquifer.

Use nearby Rye, Beulah Valley, Gardner, Walsenburg, Salt Creek, and Pueblo as broader context, but give the greatest weight to wells with similar geology and elevation. Have a driller review access and the proposed well location before purchase. If the property will include livestock, irrigation, or a new home, confirm the permit conditions and any augmentation requirements. Plan the well, septic system, driveway, electrical service, and house site together so one does not block another.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Colorado City, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth near Colorado City is 250 feet. The middle half runs from 95 to 475 feet, while the 90th percentile is 605 feet. About 27% are under 100 feet and 11% exceed 600 feet. A nearby well is useful for planning, but local depth can change sharply between parcels.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Colorado City?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 250-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $8,800 to $13,800. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $14,800 to $25,800. Access, extra casing, geology, and utility distance can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Colorado City?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 10.0 gallons-per-minute median, with the middle half from 6.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 2% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 11% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. Request the actual yield and recovery test for the property instead of relying only on area statistics.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Colorado City?
faq.a: The local map shows 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, 1 historic mine feature, and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped locations do not determine water quality at a specific lot. Test an existing or new well for bacteria, nitrates, and contaminants relevant to the property before drinking it.

faq.q: Are Colorado City wells getting deeper or losing water?
faq.a: The limited static-level record does not show a simple decline. Median measured water depth was 203 feet below surface in the 2010s and 105 feet in the 2020s, indicating shallower measurements in the newer group. Only 37 wells report static water levels, so a current measurement from the specific well is more useful than a broad trend.
